name: SupplyChainCompromise
description: A case template for investigating suspected or confirmed supply chain or third-party compromise incidents, including compromised software, updates, vendors, managed service providers, or trusted third-party access paths.
author: Zachary Carter
summary:
## Incident Report — [CASE TITLE]

## Executive Summary

**[Provide a high-level, non-technical summary suitable for senior leadership and stakeholders. Describe the nature of the supply chain or third-party compromise, how and when it was identified, the estimated scope of impact to this organization, key findings, and current response status. Clarify whether this organization is a victim, a potential downstream source of impact to others, or both. Typically two to four paragraphs.]**

## Scope of Investigation

**[Define the boundaries of this investigation. Identify which vendor, software, update, or third-party access path is the subject of this case. Document what was in-scope, what was explicitly excluded, and any limitations on access or evidence — including dependency on the vendor for information — that constrained findings.]**

## Analysis — MITRE ATT&CK® Framework

**[Map investigative findings to the MITRE ATT&CK framework (https://attack.mitre.org). In supply chain cases, many initial access and execution techniques may have occurred within the vendor environment and may not be directly observable. Document what is confirmed within your environment versus what is assessed or reported by the vendor or external intelligence.]**

**[Complete each subsection with specific techniques, evidence, and timeline data. Remove tactics where no activity was observed and note the absence explicitly.]**

### TA0001 — Initial Access

**Techniques observed:**

**[e.g. T1195.001 Compromise Software Dependencies and Development Tools, T1195.002 Compromise Software Supply Chain, T1199 Trusted Relationship]**

**[Describe how the threat actor introduced the compromise — via a software update, build pipeline, compromised vendor access, or malicious dependency. Note whether initial access occurred in your environment or was inherited via a trusted third party. Document the delivery mechanism, affected software or vendor, and the earliest evidence of malicious activity in your environment.]**

| Date/Time (UTC) | Technique | Host / Account | Description | Evidence Source |
|-----------------|-----------|---------------|-------------|----------------|
| | | | | |

### TA0002 — Execution

**Techniques observed:**

**[e.g. T1059.001 PowerShell, T1072 Software Deployment Tools, T1569.002 Service Execution]**

**[Document how malicious code was executed in your environment following the supply chain compromise. Include the trusted mechanism used — software installer, update agent, deployment tool, vendor script, etc.]**

| Date/Time (UTC) | Technique | Host | Command / Binary | Evidence Source |
|-----------------|-----------|------|-----------------|----------------|
| | | | | |

### TA0003 — Persistence

**Techniques observed:**

**[e.g. T1053.005 Scheduled Task, T1543.003 Windows Service, T1547.001 Registry Run Keys, T1136 Create Account]**

**[Describe mechanisms used to maintain access. In supply chain cases, persistence is often established through the compromised software itself or via backdoors introduced during the build process.]**

| Date/Time (UTC) | Technique | Host | Artifact / Path | Status |
|-----------------|-----------|------|----------------|--------|
| | | | | Confirmed / Removed / Pending |

### TA0004 — Privilege Escalation

**Techniques observed:**

**[e.g. T1078 Valid Accounts, T1068 Exploitation for Privilege Escalation]**

**[Detail how the threat actor elevated privileges within your environment following execution of the compromised component.]**

| Date/Time (UTC) | Technique | Host | Account | Privilege Reached | Evidence Source |
|-----------------|-----------|------|---------|-----------------|----------------|
| | | | | | |

### TA0005 — Defense Evasion

**Techniques observed:**

**[e.g. T1036 Masquerading, T1070 Indicator Removal, T1562.001 Disable Security Tools, T1553.002 Code Signing]**

**[Describe techniques used to avoid detection. In supply chain cases, the threat actor commonly abuses code-signing certificates, trusted update mechanisms, and legitimate software to evade detection.]**

| Date/Time (UTC) | Technique | Host | Description | Evidence Source |
|-----------------|-----------|------|-------------|----------------|
| | | | | |

### TA0006 — Credential Access

**Techniques observed:**

**[e.g. T1003.001 LSASS Memory, T1558.003 Kerberoasting, T1552 Unsecured Credentials]**

**[Document methods used to harvest credentials and the scope of accounts exposed within your environment.]**

| Date/Time (UTC) | Technique | Host | Accounts Compromised | Evidence Source |
|-----------------|-----------|------|---------------------|----------------|
| | | | | |

### TA0007 — Discovery

**Techniques observed:**

**[e.g. T1087.002 Domain Account Enumeration, T1046 Network Scanning, T1135 Network Share Discovery, T1018 Remote System Discovery]**

**[Describe internal reconnaissance conducted after the compromised component established a foothold.]**

| Date/Time (UTC) | Technique | Host | Tool / Method | Scope |
|-----------------|-----------|------|--------------|-------|
| | | | | |

### TA0008 — Lateral Movement

**Techniques observed:**

**[e.g. T1021.001 RDP, T1021.002 SMB/Windows Admin Shares, T1570 Lateral Tool Transfer]**

**[Detail how the threat actor moved from the initial foothold — often a widely deployed agent or software component — to additional systems.]**

| Date/Time (UTC) | Technique | Source Host | Destination Host | Account Used | Evidence Source |
|-----------------|-----------|------------|-----------------|--------------|----------------|
| | | | | | |

### TA0009 — Collection

**Techniques observed:**

**[e.g. T1074.001 Local Data Staging, T1560 Archive Collected Data, T1213 Data from Information Repositories]**

**[Document any data staging, archiving, or targeting of sensitive information repositories prior to exfiltration.]**

| Date/Time (UTC) | Technique | Host | Path / Target | Volume | Evidence Source |
|-----------------|-----------|------|--------------|--------|-----------------|
| | | | | | |

### TA0011 — Command and Control

**Techniques observed:**

**[e.g. T1071.001 Web Protocols, T1071.004 DNS, T1573 Encrypted Channel, T1102 Web Service]**

**[Document C2 infrastructure, protocols, and beaconing behaviour. In supply chain cases, C2 may be embedded within legitimate-looking update traffic or use infrastructure designed to blend with expected vendor communications.]**

| Indicator | Type | Protocol / Port | First Seen (UTC) | Last Seen (UTC) |
|-----------|------|----------------|-----------------|----------------|
| | IP / Domain / URL | | | |

### TA0010 — Exfiltration

**Techniques observed:**

**[e.g. T1041 Exfiltration Over C2 Channel, T1048 Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol, T1567 Exfiltration Over Web Service]**

**Exfiltration confirmed:** <!-- Yes / No / Under investigation -->

**Estimated volume:** <!-- e.g. ~4.2 GB / Unknown -->

**[Describe staging, compression, and transfer activity observed within your environment. Note whether exfiltration destinations overlap with known vendor infrastructure or are clearly attacker-controlled.]**

| Date/Time (UTC) | Technique | Source Host | Destination | Volume | Evidence Source |
|-----------------|-----------|------------|-------------|--------|-----------------|
| | | | | | |

**Data types at risk:**

| Data Type | Location | Estimated Volume | Regulatory Classification |
|-----------|----------|-----------------|--------------------------|
| | | | |

### TA0040 — Impact to Entity

**Techniques observed:**

**[e.g. T1486 Data Encrypted for Impact, T1485 Data Destruction, T1489 Service Stop, T1490 Inhibit System Recovery]**

**[Document any destructive or disruptive actions taken within your environment as a result of the supply chain compromise.]**

| Date/Time (UTC) | Technique | Scope | Description | Evidence Source |
|-----------------|-----------|-------|-------------|----------------|
| | | | | |

---

## Cyber Threat Intelligence (CTI) Findings

**[Document CTI findings relevant to this supply chain incident. Include threat actor attribution (if known), campaign associations, affected software or vendor advisories, and any public reporting or government advisories associated with this compromise. Note whether CISA, NCSC, or vendor-issued advisories are applicable.]**

### Threat Actor Profile

**Suspected group / alias:** <!-- e.g. APT29 / Cozy Bear / UNC2452 / Unknown -->

**Attribution confidence:** <!-- High / Moderate / Low / Unattributed -->

**Assessed motivation:** <!-- Espionage / Financial / Sabotage / Unknown -->

**ATT&CK Group:** <!-- e.g. G0016 -->

**[Provide a narrative summary of the suspected or confirmed threat actor, including known aliases, affiliation, prior supply chain campaigns, and links to public reporting or government advisories.]**

| Intelligence Source | Reference | Relevance |
|--------------------|-----------|----------|
| | | |

### Vendor / Software Advisory

| Vendor | Product / Component | Advisory Reference | CVE(s) | Patch Available | Applied |
|--------|--------------------|--------------------|--------|----------------|--------|
| | | | | Yes / No / Pending | Yes / No / Pending |

---

## Downstream Impact Assessment

**[Assess whether your organization may have propagated the compromise to downstream customers, partners, or managed environments through your own software, services, or access paths. This is a critical and often-overlooked dimension of supply chain cases.]**

**Downstream propagation risk:** <!-- Confirmed / Suspected / Not applicable / Under assessment -->

| Downstream Party | Relationship | Exposure Type | Notified? | Date |
|-----------------|-------------|---------------|-----------|------|
| | Customer / Partner / Subsidiary | Software / Access / Data | Yes / No / Pending | |

---

## Remediation & Recommendations

**[Prioritised remediation actions to contain the incident, eradicate the threat, and prevent recurrence.]**

### Immediate Actions

| # | Action | Owner | Priority | Due |
|---|--------|-------|----------|-----|
| 1 | Isolate or block the compromised software component or vendor access path across all affected systems | | Critical | |
| 2 | Identify all systems running the affected software version or connected via the compromised vendor account | | Critical | |
| 3 | Reset credentials for all accounts accessible to or via the compromised component or vendor | | Critical | |
| 4 | Preserve forensic evidence and engage legal counsel for regulatory and downstream notification obligations | | Critical | |
| 5 | Apply vendor-issued patches or mitigations and validate integrity of replacement components | | High | |
| 6 | Audit and revoke unnecessary third-party access, API keys, and service account permissions | | High | |
| 7 | Deploy detection rules targeting observed TTPs and IOCs across SIEM and EDR | | High | |

### Strategic Improvements

| # | Recommendation | Category | Priority |
|---|---------------|----------|----------|
| 1 | Implement a formal software supply chain risk management program including vendor security assessments | Governance | High |
| 2 | Enforce software provenance verification — code signing validation, SBOM review, and hash verification for critical components | Architecture | High |
| 3 | Apply least-privilege to all third-party access paths, API integrations, and vendor accounts | Identity | High |
| 4 | Establish a vendor breach notification protocol and include supply chain breach scenarios in IR planning | Preparedness | High |
| 5 | Implement network segmentation to limit blast radius of trusted software components and vendor access | Architecture | Medium |
| 6 | Conduct tabletop exercises specifically modelling supply chain compromise scenarios | Preparedness | Medium |

---

## Conclusion

**[Closing summary reinforcing key findings, overall impact, and the path forward. Suitable for sharing with executive leadership. Address the nature of the supply chain compromise, what was confirmed within your environment, estimated dwell time, whether downstream notification obligations were triggered, and confidence in containment and recovery.]**

tasks.title: Validate supply chain compromise and classify incident
tasks.description: Confirm whether a supply chain or third-party compromise has affected your environment. Identify the affected vendor, software, update, or access path. Classify the incident as confirmed compromise, suspected exposure, precautionary investigation, or false positive. Document the source of initial notification — vendor advisory, threat intelligence, internal detection, government alert, or third-party notification.

tasks.title: Identify affected software, versions, and deployment scope
tasks.description: Enumerate all systems, services, and environments running the affected software version or component. Identify deployment methods — managed update, manual install, container image, CI/CD pipeline, package dependency. Document version numbers, deployment dates, and whether automatic updates were enabled.

tasks.title: Initiate incident communications and escalation
tasks.description: Notify required internal stakeholders and activate the appropriate incident response, management, legal, privacy, communications, and executive escalation paths. Brief leadership on the nature of supply chain compromise and the dependency on vendor-provided information. Engage legal counsel early given potential downstream notification obligations.

tasks.title: Preserve forensic evidence
tasks.description: Collect and preserve volatile and non-volatile evidence from affected systems. Prioritise EDR telemetry, process execution logs, network connection logs, authentication logs, and scheduled task and service artifacts associated with the compromised component. Preserve software installer or update artifacts for hash validation and binary analysis.

tasks.title: Assess vendor communication and advisory status
tasks.description: Engage the vendor formally to obtain advisory details, IOCs, affected version ranges, patch availability, and recommended mitigations. Track all vendor communications. Obtain written confirmation of the compromise scope and any forensic assistance offered. Monitor for updated advisories from the vendor, CISA, NCSC, or relevant CERTs.

tasks.title: Investigate malicious activity within your environment
tasks.description: Investigate what activity the threat actor conducted within your environment following the supply chain compromise. Identify execution of malicious code, C2 communications, internal reconnaissance, lateral movement, credential access, data staging, and exfiltration. Do not assume the scope is limited to what the vendor has disclosed.

tasks.title: Contain affected systems and third-party access
tasks.description: Isolate or block the compromised software component or vendor access path. Disable or revoke affected vendor accounts, API keys, tokens, and integrations. Block confirmed malicious infrastructure at network boundaries. Restrict lateral movement paths from systems running the affected component.

tasks.title: Investigate privilege escalation and lateral movement
tasks.description: Determine whether the threat actor elevated privileges or moved laterally from the initial foothold established via the compromised component. Assess whether domain controllers, identity infrastructure, backup systems, or sensitive data repositories were reached.

tasks.title: Assess data access and exfiltration risk
tasks.description: Determine whether sensitive data was accessed, staged, or exfiltrated. Identify data types at risk, regulatory classification, and whether the data exposure triggers notification obligations under HIPAA or applicable US state privacy laws.

tasks.title: Assess downstream propagation risk
tasks.description: Determine whether your organization may have propagated the compromise to customers, partners, or managed environments through your own software, services, or access. Identify downstream parties at risk and assess notification obligations. This is a critical and often-overlooked dimension of supply chain incidents.

tasks.title: Extract, validate, and track IOCs
tasks.description: Extract and validate indicators of compromise from malware artifacts, host evidence, network telemetry, vendor advisories, and external intelligence. Add confirmed IOCs to the case and share with downstream systems as authorized. Cross-reference vendor-published IOCs against your own telemetry.

tasks.title: Eradicate malicious artifacts and remediate access
tasks.description: Remove or replace the compromised software component with a validated clean version. Remove malicious artifacts, persistence mechanisms, backdoors, and unauthorized accounts. Revoke and rotate all credentials and tokens accessible to the compromised component or vendor. Patch or mitigate all exploited vulnerabilities.

tasks.title: Validate software integrity and restore systems
tasks.description: Verify the integrity of replacement software components using vendor-provided hashes, signatures, or SBOMs. Restore affected systems from validated clean baselines where reimage is required. Validate restored functionality and apply enhanced monitoring.

tasks.title: Assess external reporting and notification obligations
tasks.description: Determine whether regulators, law enforcement, cyber insurance, customers, or partners must be notified based on HIPAA, applicable US state privacy laws, contractual obligations, or policy requirements. Assess both upstream obligations (to regulators) and downstream obligations (to affected customers and partners).

tasks.title: Strengthen third-party risk and supply chain controls
tasks.description: Implement security improvements to reduce supply chain risk, including software provenance verification, vendor access controls, least-privilege for integrations, SBOM adoption, and enhanced monitoring of third-party software behavior.

tasks.title: Conduct lessons learned and close case
tasks.description: Document root cause, response actions, business impact, vendor handling, downstream impact, and improvement opportunities. Confirm recovery is complete, no ongoing malicious activity is observed, required notifications are resolved, and closure criteria are met.
